utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, can the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, case number ^ IT-95-17/1 PT, the Prosecutor versus Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the accused hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. FURUNDZIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I have appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: For the Office of the Prosecutor, I appear; my name is Michael Blaxill, I am accompanied by my learned friend Ms. Patricia Sellers and our case manager Ms. Udo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Luka Misetic on behalf of the defendant. Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all, there is the motion of the Defence on the defects in the indictment. Although the Prosecutor did respond, it was out of time and the Chamber has decided not to take it into consideration. However, if the Defence counsel wishes to make any oral submissions on the motion -- and we have received the authorities that accompanied your motion -- and if you wish to say anything in support of your motion, you are free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I prepared an oral argument and, if it pleases the court I would go ahead and proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May it please the court, good morning, President Mumba, Judge Cassese, Judge May. This morning, 29 April 1998, Anto Furundzija asks you to invoke the powers bestowed upon you by the Statute of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to dismiss all charges against him and to allow him to return to his home country immediately. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was established to punish serious violations of international humanitarian law, including such crimes as genocide, murder and systematic rape. The Tribunal is here to ensure that the architects and engineers of such policies as ethnic cleansing do not escape justice. However, contrary to the beliefs of many commentators, scholars and others in the general public the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia is not here simply to punish violations of international humanitarian law. Rather, the ICTY is here to ensure that the rule of law is respected and enforced. By focusing on the enforcement of the rule of law, human rights are advanced by punishing the ethnic cleansers, but also advanced by strenuously and zealously protecting the rights of the individuals brought before the Tribunal. One such individual, Anto Furundzija, today asks you, the guardians of the rule of law, to give life to the rights enshrined in Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal and to the rights enshrined in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. A brief history of this case to date, your Honours -- as you will recall, the Defence previously filed a motion to dismiss for vagueness in February of this year. That motion was heard by this Trial Chamber on 9 March 1998. The Trial Chamber denied the motion, but ordered that the Prosecutor: "Specify how the accused, Anto Furundzija, is alleged to have violated Article 7(1) of the Tribunal." The Defence submits that the Prosecutor failed to abide by that order. Instead, the Prosecutor filed a document entitled, "Prosecutor's reply, re Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal" which enumerates many possible theories they may use at trial against Mr. Furundzija but includes no additional facts and in no way specifies how Mr. Furundzija specifically and factually violated Article 7(1). The Prosecutor does not commit to any theory of liability under Article 7(1) and, in fact, in one paragraph at the end, somewhat unbelievably to the Defence, includes a paragraph which says we reserve the right to come up with a new theory of liability at trial, including one we have not disclosed to you previously but which may arise during the course of the proceedings. Nevertheless, despite the Defence's contention that that document is a violation of the order entered by this Tribunal, it is clear that the Prosecutor now intends to pursue any one of six potential theories of liability under Article 7(1), that Mr. Furundzija planned, instigated, ordered, aided and abetted in the planning, aided and abetted in the preparation, and aided and abetted in the execution of the rape of Witness A. It is the Defence's contention that, with respect to the first five possible theories of liability, those charges must be dismissed for vagueness. Indeed, "vague" is too soft a word. There are absolutely no factual allegations in the indictment, in the reply filed by the Prosecutor or in the supporting materials to support an allegation, or even an inference, that Mr. Furundzija in any way planned the rape, ordered the rape, instigated the rape, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning or instigating or ordering of the rape -- none. As a matter of fact, the indictment specifically states that Witness A was raped at least four times prior to Mr. Furundzija's mention in the indictment. That is the same with respect to the supporting materials that were disclosed to the Defence and filed in this case. How and from where the Prosecutor draws the conclusion that he ordered, planned, instigated or aided and/or abetted in the planning, ordering or instigation is not evident from the documents and, more importantly, is absolutely not clear to the Defence. The Defence would submit that under Article 21 the Defence is entitled to know the factual basis upon which such allegations could be brought, so that we could prepare. Specifically, we are entitled to know if there was a planning, if they intend to pursue that theory, and ordering and instigating, who did it, when did it happen, where did it happen, with whom did it happen, et cetera. There are no factual allegations to support such a conclusion and, on that basis, we ask that the first five theories of liability be dismissed. With respect to the sixth potential theory of liability under Article 7(1), there are some factual allegations made in the indictment and in the supporting materials from which, if proven at trial, they could make an argument for aiding and abetting in the execution. First, let me preface this argument by saying that the Defence, and Mr. Furundzija in particular, strenuously deny the factual allegations in the indictment and in the supporting materials against him. Nevertheless, for the purposes of this motion only, we concede every factual allegation made in the indictment and made in the supporting materials. We are asking you to draw a legal conclusion as to the sufficiency of these factual allegations. The allegations in the indictment and the supporting materials to support the potential aiding and abetting and the execution are as follows. The person whom I will refer to as "Defendant A" allegedly raped Witness A four times on or about 15 May 1993. The indictment alleges that other individuals brought Witness A to a specific location, that Defendant A then appeared, Defendant A engaged in a series of acts, including rape, including, I believe, physical abuse of Witness A, et cetera, et cetera. The indictment then alleges that Mr. Furundzija appeared on the scene, asked Witness A a couple of questions, and then was present while Defendant A again raped Witness A. The indictment states that Mr. Furundzija then allegedly left the scene and, over the course of apparently the next two months, Defendant A continued to engage in this conduct repeatedly for what appears in the indictment and in the supporting material to be dozens of occasions. The question before this Trial Chamber now is, in a theory for aiding and abetting in the execution, what is the threshold standard for liability? In the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber there, in its judgement, reviewed the state of international law, and determined that an individual can only be guilty of aiding and abetting in the execution if the individual directly and substantially facilitated the rape of an individual -- in this case directly and substantially facilitated the rape of Witness A in some significant way. Significantly enough, the Prosecutor has conceded in the brief, which I understand now will not be considered by the court, but the Prosecutor has conceded that that indeed is the standard. This is a standard also enumerated in the ILC draft code as referenced in the defendant's brief. Therefore, the issue before the court is, is Mr. Furundzija's presence, and the fact that he allegedly asked a couple of questions of Witness A -- does that rise to the level of direct and substantial facilitation of the rape of Witness A by Defendant A in some significant way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I follow the argument, Mr. Misetic, but is that not just a matter of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Is it not going to be a matter, if the Prosecution is putting the case in the way you suggest they are, and of course we must determine whether or not that is so, but if that is the case, is it not then a matter of evidence for a court to determine whether that standard has been reached on the evidence; is it possible to draw the inference or not, rather than at this stage trying to have the entire indictment quashed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would contend absolutely not. The reason is as follows: as I have stated before, we are conceding for the purposes of this motion every factual allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, as you must.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. So the fact of the matter is you will be faced then at the close of trial or at the close of the Prosecutor's case -- you will be in the exact same position as you would be today. In fact, the Prosecutor's case today will be better than the Prosecutor's case at the close of trial. Why? Because I will guarantee you right now I am not going to concede the facts at the time of trial. I will strenuously cross-examine the witnesses brought by the Prosecutor with respect to their veracity, with respect to their reliability, et cetera. Furthermore, if necessary, if you do not dismiss the case at the close of the Prosecutor's evidence, we will put on evidence to further contradict the allegations made in the indictment and in the supporting materials. Therefore, the Prosecutor, in effect what they are arguing here is not they should have a trial where this will become clear because it will never be better than it is today; rather, they wish -- and this is the Defence's position -- to continue on in this fog, where they cannot enumerate what Mr. Furundzija did. If you read the reply they filed with respect to Article 7(1) liability, they do not commit to a legal theory, because they do not know what the theory is. That is the basis of this motion. Why is it our position that we do not need to have a full trial? If we have conceded every factual allegation, the question before you is to make a legal determination right now as to whether these factual allegations could lead to a conclusion of aiding and abetting. If they are going to contend that there is some other factual evidence that could arise at trial which would give rise to aiding and abetting, we are entitled to know that now and we are entitled to have it in the indictment so we can prepare for it. But to suggest that they can make certain factual allegations which they are not saying is the basis for the aiding and abetting liability and that they can keep this hidden from the Defence and then spring it at trial to get aiding and abetting liability, clearly violates Article 21, because we are entitled to be fully prepared for trial, and it violates the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. They cannot have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just add this. If that were the position, if there were some evidence which was being kept back from you, and you had not received it before the trial, then clearly, in my view, you would be entitled to claim the defendant's right to a fair trial had been breached. It is clearly right that you have all the material before the trial so that you can prepare for it properly and also right that you know the way in which the Prosecution put the case. How do they put the case against your client, how do they say that he was involved in these offences -- all that is clearly so and, in due course, no doubt, we will find out. So, you need not, as far as I am concerned, trouble yourself with that aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may reply. We are on the eve of trial now -- we are inside of six weeks to the start of trial. My first contention is that that is not something that can be disclosed to the Defence in the form of a witness statement, but if the substance of the aiding and abetting liability has not been stated in the indictment, then it must be put in the indictment. What we are saying is that you cannot have factual allegations in an indictment which you now, at a motion to dismiss, say, "Well, that is not what we are really relying on to establish that the person committed the crime which we are alleging." If they are claiming that there is something else out there that is the basis for aiding and abetting liability under Article 7(1), then under every national jurisdiction that I know of and under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Articles of the Tribunal, that has to be spelt out in the indictment. We cannot wait until a week before a trial or whenever the Prosecutor decides to submit a witness statement -- (a) wait a week before trial; (b) have the Defence guess through the supporting materials or any other materials provided by the Prosecutor that this is the theory of liability under Article 7(1). We are saying it should be dismissed because, in all honesty, if the theories of liability are not in the witness statements of Witness A, I cannot imagine where they are coming up with these factual allegations. That is point 1. But point 2, we are entitled to rely on what we have been given so far -- the facts in the indictment, the supporting materials, the "clarification" provided by the Prosecutor's reply. Based on this body of documents that have been provided to us, we are saying, okay, let us review now what the allegations are. It is unfathomable to me that we can sit here today, less than six weeks before trial, and say, yes, you have this entire body; yes, you have the indictment, but we cannot rule as to what the basis for aiding and abetting liability is, because the Prosecutor would like to go to trial to see if he can figure it out. That is basically what their contention is. We are entitled to go to trial and, if you read the reply, it says -- something that I had a lot of fun with -- "The trial process is a fluid and dynamic process." I read that as code: "We want to go to trial and examine some witnesses because we may stumble upon something upon which we can then base an indictment." That is not the way that this Trial Chamber or this Tribunal should operate. If we are going to have a trial, Mr. Furundzija and I are fully prepared to go absolutely to the wall at trial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask Defence counsel to speak a little more slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you slow down for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I apologise to the translators and to the people in the booth. We are entitled not to have to wait on the eve of trial and then try to catch a butterfly with a net. They interview a witness or examine a witness and we will come up with a different theory. If you read the reply, which I would ask you to re-read, we could do this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that point has been taken. It is a long response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was responding to Judge May, though. If I may basically wind up with this: again, let me reiterate something. Their factual allegations will never be better than they are today, and to the extent then that their argument is going to be, "We are entitled to go to trial anyway," then we would say that that is a clear violation of Article 21 and our right to be prepared for trial, because we would say, "No, you are not entitled to go to trial. If I concede to you every factual allegation," then the point of a trial, your Honour, is to weigh the factual issues, because there are factual issues in doubt. That is the point of a trial. If there are no factual issues in dispute for the purposes of the motion, then (a) there is no need for a trial; and, (b), let me also state it is a gross waste of the Tribunal's resources and time then to have to have a full trial on issues that we are willing to concede right now, just so that the Prosecutor can try to figure out what they are doing at trial. On that basis, we would say that we believe absolutely that, no, they are not entitled to go to trial. Even if now they were to come up and say we have a witness statement, we would argue that five weeks before trial is a little late to be now amending your indictment and coming up with a new theory of liability -- if that is something they wanted to contend, obviously we would take that up with a different motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think that is all on this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have decided that perhaps we may give the Prosecution a right to reply, only to what has been raised in the oral arguments, because, as I indicated earlier, your response came a day late, without any reasons for the delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am much obliged for the opportunity. I will confine myself, as your Honour requires, and obviously there is an apology due to you as a Chamber and individually for a failing on the part of the Prosecution. I was proposing that perhaps that could be dealt with as a professional courtesy and as a matter of the process of the proceedings towards trial during the status conference, but if you wish a formal apology to be lodged at this point in connection with the motion, then certainly you have an unreserved apology for the untimely filing of a document by the Prosecution. The issue here, I think, is very much, as his Honour Judge May has indicated, a factual issue relating to the trial. The indictment has already been subjected to the scrutiny of a confirming judge. The indictment has already been the subject of the scrutiny of this Chamber and, indeed, a previous motion as to the form of the indictment has been denied, and the indictment stands. I will not reiterate the arguments that have already been canvassed in this case in relation to the contents of the indictment, save to say that in his address this morning, my learned friend for the Defence has concentrated very much on the issue of saying some substantial or direct contribution to the act of rape. It should be borne in mind that the allegations against the accused are those provisions relating to torture or inhumane treatment, so in fact it is not simply the level of involvement in just -- I say "just" -- that is not in any way to diminish the act, but just in the element of rape but in the overall circumstances pleaded in, now, counts 13 and 14. It is our view that, therefore, this is an issue that has previously been decided by the court. Clearly, however, I feel it is appropriate never to try and object to the airing of any fresh issue by Defence counsel -- I think it is only proper that every avenue is explored on the way to and during a trial. The simple fact here is that this present motion is borne of a document filed pursuant to the order of this court, and the document was to specify the legal theories we may advance in relation to Article 7(1) of the Statute. Article 7(1) is pleaded at paragraph 11 of the indictment, and is stated as individual criminal responsibility "includes committing, planning instigating, ordering or otherwise aiding and abetting in", et cetera. The reality is that our theory, our legal theory relating to Article 7(1) is quite simply that these elements are alternatives within a given provision. I think it would be an improper construction of the wording of that Article, I think it would be indeed, on the common meaning and the application of the words contained therein -- I think it would be perhaps to make a nonsense of the Article if one had to prove that for any criminal offence somebody committed it and planned it and instigated it and ordered it. It would seem that if somebody orders the commission of a crime, they probably are not the person committing it in the hands-on way. So, I do submit to your Honours that these are mutually independent -- they are exclusive, they are alternatives. They are independent constructions which can be applied on the evidence that the court receives and I think that is the crucial point. Turning to His Honour Judge May's remarks, it is a matter of evidence. There has been the rather perhaps trite phrase of "fluid and dynamic process" for a trial, but in point of fact I think that is so. Quite often, in the course of a trial, the evidence will be different at the end of the day to that which is anticipated by the parties at the outset. It is the natural way of things. Some witnesses will become stronger in some areas, some will forget things and appear weaker than they are anticipated by either counsel for the Prosecution or the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You may save yourself some breath. We do not need those details. We are quite acquainted with what goes on in criminal trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not mean to be impudent and try to instruct you in the duties of the court. That is essentially it. At this stage we are saying, in a sense, do we try the case by motion or do we let the trial try the case. I commend to you the latter and your previous denial for the motion of lack in the form of the indictment would indeed hold good today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Will you help us factually? As opposed to the theory of the matter, if one looks at counts 12 to 14, what is alleged is that this accused was present -- is this right -- while the other man was responsible for various indecencies and indeed a rape?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And do you invite us to draw an inference from that? Is that the way that you put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No, I would say it is far more than an inference, your Honour. The essential issue that the Prosecution say factually applies here is this: it is alleged that this lady is being held, Witness A, by members of a small unit in a building. This person indeed has been -- has suffered and been subjected to abuse. The allegation against this accused is that he, in performing his duties, enters the room where this is taking place. He commences an interrogation. In the course of interrogation, a further rape takes place. This person allegedly is also beaten. Another person, who knows her, is brought in -- both of them are beaten -- and this is, we say, forms part of the interrogation, or, rather the interrogation is laid over this abuse of the Witness A and the other person. So, we are saying that this is a direct involvement, because in the torture -- it is an element, as we understand it, of torture, that to allow some kind of physical abuse of somebody who is being held whilst trying to elicit information forms torture and therefore is a direct participation in the offence. I hope that assists, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Essentially, those are my representations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I reply very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is our strenuous objection now to the reintroduction of a torture theory of liability against Mr. Furundzija. You ordered the Prosecution to clarify what their theories of liability against Mr. Furundzija were. They filed the reply. Not one solitary word in their four-page reply about a potential theory of liability involving torture -- not one. I would contend that this pleading is a pleading which clarified the indictment and therefore we are entitled to rely on that document. That document has been filed for a month and now they want to go back, because I contend they concede, on this motion, and now want to reintroduce another theory of liability which they gave up by filing that document. My frustration with this case, your Honours, is I am five weeks at trial and they are coming up with new theories of liability, you order to specify the theories of liability, I rely on it. A month later they come back and say -- I am sure Mr. Blaxill will get up and say, "I am entitled to come back with something else now." How we are to prepare for trial if we are not entitled to get the Prosecutor to specify what the charges are against him. I object strenuously now to a torture theory of liability. Four pages and not a word about torture. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: After due consideration of the arguments by the parties, the Chamber has decided that the motion by the Defence will be declined, but the Prosecution is ordered to file a document containing factual specifications on which they intend to rely at trial as to what the accused before the court now did on the material dates and at the material times and this document must be filed by Monday, 4 May 1998. The Defence raised the issue that the document which you filed on your legal theories does not appear to be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When one takes into account what you have just submitted before the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I heard the point. We were asked specifically, indeed ordered, to explain the legal theories under Article 7(1); we did restrict ourselves to what we thought was a legal exposition. We did not in fact consider that factual representations were relevant to that exercise. My learned friend filed a comment relating to "a bill of particulars" and that is a term of art with which I am not familiar and we did not treat it as such. Clearly we will back it up with what you require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Now that the decision has been taken, I hope that the Prosecution will comply, particularly with timing, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The point is well taken, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can clarify something. With respect to the argument I made at the close, are they now going to be entitled to re-raise the issue of torture?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They are entitled to raise whatever theory they are going to rely on at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Even though they gave up that theory in the last pleading filed in the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They are being given a chance now to deal with their case properly, to specify the factual situations and also to specify the legal theory they are going to rely on at trial. When that document comes, that is the document which the Trial Chamber, as well as the Defence, would rely on, for the purposes of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We now have another motion by the Defence, which is dealing with the fact that, since the other statements for the other witnesses were not filed, they will not be heard at the trial. This motion is unfortunately tied up with the Prosecution's motion for protective measures which deals with the type of witnesses they have and the type of protection they are asking from the Trial Chamber, and, because of this, the two were filed on the same date -- 24 April -- so we believe it is better to deal with these issues in the status conference which is to follow immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If it was filed on the 24th, I have no copy of it. I checked my mailbox this morning before I walked in -- nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What happened with service?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That particular protective motion was filed ex parte, so indeed Mr. Misetic would not have a copy in his possession at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will move on to the status conference, which will be in closed session.
